{"artifact":"SmeDossierEnvelope","schema_version":"0.4.0","stage_id":"02.dossier_sections","probe":"rdmv-hi-x","lineage":{"input_manifest_sha256":"7b008df13801c6f141cdb32d7a10acc7fbe1b2d217226946527c0cc3c5b0b098","candidate_lineage_id":"2026-10-28-rdmv-hi-class-3:lineage:55","source_registry_sha256":"1323c0f691f132d6e9e9a263c68306b972b82c8bbaa5a48a33a79177660764be","source_liveness_sha256":"27cf6d56fae2d5323c61bcbb69f0d992aeceb71a7dae4302b1f14baa17651cb0"},"envelope_scope":{"kind":"partial_chunk","assigned_section_ids":["C"],"chunk_index":1,"chunk_total":1},"section_char_limit":12000,"sections":[{"section_id":"C","chunk_id":"C.01","merge_seq":1,"domain":"Backing, Entering Traffic, Roundabouts, Lanes, Speed, Turns, Passing, Stopping and Brakes","heading":"C — Backing, Entering Traffic, Roundabouts, Lanes, Speed, Turns, Passing, Stopping and Brakes","learner_facing":true,"markdown":"## C — Backing, Entering Traffic, Roundabouts, Lanes, Speed, Turns, Passing, Stopping and Brakes

FACT_ID: sec13-F01 | anchor: A01
Hawaii law forbids a driver or any adult passenger from leaving a child under nine years old unattended in a motor vehicle for five minutes or longer, because of dangers such as extreme heat, theft of the car, or accidental use of the emergency brake, power windows or trunk release [A01].
Why it matters: under nine and five minutes are the two numbers in the unattended-child law.
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0064]

FACT_ID: sec13-F02 | anchor: A01
Backing is dangerous because visibility is restricted, so check the area behind the vehicle before getting in, turn around and look to the rear instead of relying on mirrors whose view is too small, and have someone outside guide you if you cannot see [A01].
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0064]

FACT_ID: sec13-F03 | anchor: A01
When backing, apply the brakes gently as the movement starts to confirm they work, always back slowly, watch the front of the vehicle for clearance when backing and turning at once, and avoid backing into or across a roadway, parking so that you can enter traffic forward [A01].
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0064]

FACT_ID: sec13-F04 | anchor: A01
When traffic is clear, back only into the lane nearest the edge of the roadway, and the chief responsibility for avoiding a collision rests with the driver leaving a parking space, who should look, signal and yield [A01].
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0064]

FACT_ID: sec13-F05 | anchor: A01
Use extraordinary caution when backing in residential areas, because children often play behind and between parked vehicles [A01].
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0064]

FACT_ID: sec13-F06 | anchor: A01
Entering from a driveway you must always stop before crossing the sidewalk area, since failing to stop is unlawful, then move forward slowly watching for pedestrians and vehicles, make sure the lane is clear, enter the nearest lane with a right turn when possible, and accelerate to traffic speed [A01].
Why it matters: the required stop is before the sidewalk, not at the curb line.
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0064]

FACT_ID: sec13-F07 | anchor: A02
From a parallel parking space you move forward into the nearest lane when there is enough gap in traffic, while leaving a diagonal space requires backing into the lane first, a much more dangerous and difficult maneuver that takes more time [A02].
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0065]

FACT_ID: sec13-F08 | anchor: A02
A roundabout is a one-way circular intersection serving drivers, pedestrians, pedestrians with disabilities and bicyclists, in which entering traffic must yield to circulating traffic, and each approach carries a yield sign and may have yield line markings [A02].
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0065]

FACT_ID: sec13-F09 | anchor: A02
Driving a roundabout, slow on approach, yield to pedestrians and bicyclists when entering and exiting, look left and yield to traffic already circulating including bicyclists, drive to the right of the central island counterclockwise at low speed, signal right to exit, and if you miss your exit go around again [A02].
Why it matters: look left, yield to circulating traffic and signal right to exit are the testable steps.
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0065]

FACT_ID: sec13-F10 | anchor: A02
With one lane in your direction you must use it, taking great care in congested areas, and with two lanes in open free-flowing traffic you use the right lane and the left lane only for passing or when vehicles are entering from the right, while in heavy traffic you may use either lane but keep up with traffic at a steady speed without lane hopping [A02].
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0065]

FACT_ID: sec13-F11 | anchor: A02
With three or more lanes in your direction, choose the center lanes where there are fewer conflicts, leave the right and left lanes for vehicles entering and leaving, keep a steady speed with the flow with few lane changes, and use the right lane if you are slower than other traffic [A02].
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0065]

FACT_ID: sec13-F12 | anchor: A02
Lane changes should be kept to a minimum, and before one you check conditions ahead, to the sides and behind using the mirrors and a physical head-turn check of the blind spots, then signal well in advance, the law requiring a signal for at least one hundred feet before the change begins [A02].
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0065]

FACT_ID: sec13-F13 | anchor: A03
With ample clearance, move gradually and steadily into the other lane, because abrupt movements can cause overcontrol or loss of control, and it is better to slow slightly and move in behind a vehicle, keeping it in sight, than to speed up and cut in ahead [A03].
Source: [A03 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0066]

FACT_ID: sec13-F14 | anchor: A03
Never force your way into a gap at or below the minimum safe following distance, because that discourteous move makes other drivers close ranks against you, whereas allowing time and signaling properly leads courteous drivers to make room [A03].
Source: [A03 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0066]

FACT_ID: sec13-F15 | anchor: A03
Always yield to vehicles in the other lane when changing lanes, join a congested lane at the end of the line rather than crowding in ahead, stay in your lane until the change can be made safely even if inconvenient, and never change lanes while approaching or moving through an intersection or crosswalk [A03].
Why it matters: the intersection and crosswalk ban on lane changes is a frequent test item.
Source: [A03 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0066]

FACT_ID: sec13-F16 | anchor: A03
Excessive speed for conditions is the most often listed cause of crashes, its underlying cause, whether intoxication, inattention or competition, is controlled directly by the driver, and most vehicles can reach speeds far beyond what the driver, the road and the vehicle can handle [A03].
Source: [A03 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0066]

FACT_ID: sec13-F17 | anchor: A03
A safe vehicle speed is adjusted to traffic, weather and road conditions and always stays within the posted limits [A03].
Source: [A03 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0066]

FACT_ID: sec13-F18 | anchor: A04
Keep pace with traffic, because vehicles moving the same direction at the same speed never collide while moving faster than traffic creates constant conflicts, and if you cannot keep up, move as far right as possible [A04].
Source: [A04 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0067]

FACT_ID: sec13-F19 | anchor: A04
Striking the vehicle ahead is one of the most common crashes and usually comes from following too closely, so check your interval by noting when the vehicle ahead passes a tree, pole or other marker and counting one thousand one, one thousand two, and if you reach the word two before you reach the marker you have at least the two-second interval you should never go below [A04].
Why it matters: the two-second count is the manual's following-distance rule.
Source: [A04 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0067]

FACT_ID: sec13-F20 | anchor: A04
Following too closely cuts your view of road and traffic conditions ahead, constantly changing speed confuses other drivers and bursts of speed with heavy braking are wasteful and dangerous, so maintain a steady speed [A04].
Source: [A04 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0067]

FACT_ID: sec13-F21 | anchor: A04
Reduce speed in poor road or weather conditions for better control and more time to react, and never let emotions set your speed, because being in a hurry may mean never arriving at all [A04].
Source: [A04 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0067]

FACT_ID: sec13-F22 | anchor: A04
Turns are changes of direction from a lane at intersections or driveways while curves are changes in the direction of the road itself, and for a turn you get into the proper lane well in advance, turn from the lane nearest the turn direction into the nearest available lane, and if you are in the wrong lane continue on and turn elsewhere rather than forcing a last-minute lane change [A04].
Source: [A04 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0067]

FACT_ID: sec13-F23 | anchor: A04
Make precise turns without swinging wide or cutting short, slow to a proper speed before a curve or turn and hold a steady speed through it, because braking or an abrupt speed change in a turn or curve can cause loss of control [A04].
Source: [A04 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0067]

FACT_ID: sec13-F24 | anchor: A04
Avoid left turns and U-turns whenever possible because they conflict more with traffic, are much more hazardous than right turns and impede other vehicles [A04].
Source: [A04 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0067]

FACT_ID: sec13-F25 | anchor: A04
When waiting to turn left at a red light and the light turns green, move slowly into the intersection with the wheels pointed straight ahead and turn only when the intersection is clear and it is safe [A04].
Why it matters: straight wheels protect you from being pushed into oncoming traffic if struck from behind.
Source: [A04 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0067]

FACT_ID: sec13-F26 | anchor: A04
Watch with great care for pedestrians, bicyclists and motorcyclists when turning, since vehicles, darkness or weather may hide them, always come to a complete stop before a right turn on a red signal, use extra caution on curves and turns in poor weather or on gravel, sand or mud, and do not drive in a bike lane when turning right at an intersection [A04].
Source: [A04 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0067]

FACT_ID: sec13-F27 | anchor: A05
Passing is hazardous on two or three lane roads because the opposing lane must be used and improper procedure can cause a head-on collision, so pass only when the vehicle ahead is moving below the safe speed, never merely because it is there or to gain a few car lengths in moderate or heavy traffic, and in a line of vehicles let those ahead pass the leader first [A05].
Source: [A05 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0068]

FACT_ID: sec13-F28 | anchor: A05
Pass on the left except when the vehicle being overtaken is making or about to make a left turn, in which case pass carefully on the right but never by driving onto the shoulder, and obey every sign and marking that restricts passing [A05].
Source: [A05 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0068]

FACT_ID: sec13-F29 | anchor: A05
To pass, keep enough following distance to see opposing traffic, check ahead for conflicting traffic, signal left, physically check behind for anyone passing you, sound the horn so the driver ahead knows, accelerate to passing speed in your own lane, then move left and pass [A05].
Source: [A05 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0068]

FACT_ID: sec13-F30 | anchor: A05
If a conflict appears before the pass is complete, brake sharply and drop back behind the overtaken vehicle instead of speeding up, because speed can be cut more quickly with the brakes than it can be gained with power, and return to your lane only when the overtaken vehicle is visible in your interior rear-view mirror [A05].
Why it matters: abort by braking, and the interior mirror test tells you when it is safe to pull back in.
Source: [A05 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0068]

FACT_ID: sec13-F31 | anchor: A05
Where two or more lanes run in your direction, never use an opposing lane to pass; pass on either side with proper lane change procedure, being extra careful on the right because you approach in the other driver's blind spot, and in every passing situation never pass while approaching or moving through an intersection or crosswalk [A05].
Source: [A05 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0068]

FACT_ID: sec13-F32 | anchor: A06
Parked cars block your view of vehicles, bicycles and pedestrians and may pull out or open a door into your path, so watch for movement in or near the vehicle, lit stop, back-up or signal lamps, exhaust smoke or vapor, and turning front wheels, and assume a driver who has just parked will open the door [A06].
Source: [A06 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0069]

FACT_ID: sec13-F33 | anchor: A06
Stopping unnecessarily in a traffic lane is dangerous, discourteous, inconsiderate and illegal, so stops to load or unload or to talk with others must be made in a parking space, loading zone or other place out of the lane [A06].
Source: [A06 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0069]

FACT_ID: sec13-F34 | anchor: A06
Do not stop within an intersection or crosswalk, and never drive into an intersection or crosswalk unless there is room for your entire vehicle on the far side [A06].
Source: [A06 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0069]

FACT_ID: sec13-F35 | anchor: A06
Brakes stop a vehicle by turning its energy of motion into wasted heat, so every braking wastes fuel money and wears brakes and tires, and careful braking without bursts of speed followed by hard stops saves energy and money [A06].
Source: [A06 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0069]

FACT_ID: sec13-F36 | anchor: A06
A hard brake application can make wheels slide, and sliding wheels, especially the front ones, leave you without control of the vehicle [A06].
Source: [A06 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0069]

FACT_ID: sec13-F37 | anchor: A07
When in danger of hitting a vehicle, person or object, do not jam on the brakes and slide the wheels, because you will almost certainly hit it; instead apply and release the brakes rapidly and steer toward a clear area, even off the road, while avoiding people, trees, utility poles and solid structures, and consult the owner's manual for antilock brakes [A07].
Why it matters: pump and steer is the manual's emergency braking rule for vehicles without antilock brakes.
Source: [A07 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0070]

FACT_ID: sec13-F38 | anchor: A07
Avoid braking while turning by slowing beforehand, brake very cautiously on water, ice, snow, frost, sand or gravel, and after driving through water test the brakes and, if they are weakened, apply them lightly several times until normal action returns [A07].
Source: [A07 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0070]

FACT_ID: sec13-F39 | anchor: A07
Resting your foot on the brake pedal lights the stop lamps and misleads following drivers and also partly applies the brakes in many vehicles, causing excessive wear, and a brake warning lamp that lights when you brake means a partial failure needing immediate repair [A07].
Source: [A07 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0070]

FACT_ID: sec13-F40 | anchor: A07
Begin slowing as soon as braking ahead becomes apparent, brake smoothly and steadily, and when stopping in traffic stay far enough back to see where the rear tires of the vehicle ahead meet the road, which leaves room to go around if it cannot move [A07].
Source: [A07 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0070]

FACT_ID: sec13-F41 | anchor: A07
Prolonged braking heats the brakes and makes them much less effective, which can usually be avoided by shifting to a lower gear so the engine helps hold the speed down [A07].
Source: [A07 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0070]

FACT_ID: sec13-F42 | anchor: A07
Downshifting means selecting a lower gear range while moving, works with manual and automatic transmissions, and serves two purposes, greater engine braking when slowing or holding speed on a downgrade and better performance when accelerating [A07].
Source: [A07 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0070]

FACT_ID: sec13-F43 | anchor: A07
Downshift for engine braking before starting down a steep grade because shifting is harder at higher speeds, and on a synchronized manual transmission the procedure is to depress the clutch, move the lever to the next lower gear and release the clutch slowly, while double clutching on a non-synchronized transmission should not be tried without practice [A07].
Source: [A07 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0070]

Misconceptions: when a pass goes wrong you brake and drop back rather than speeding up to finish; the lane-change signal is required for at least one hundred feet, like a turn signal; you never change lanes or pass while approaching or in an intersection or crosswalk; an abandoned pass is judged safe to end only when the overtaken vehicle shows in the interior mirror; in a roundabout you look left and yield to circulating traffic and signal right to leave; in an emergency stop you pump and steer rather than locking the wheels; waiting to turn left you keep the wheels straight, not turned.

Mnemonics: One thousand one, one thousand two is the following interval; look left, go right of the island, signal right to leave the roundabout; brake and drop back when a pass fails; pump and steer in an emergency; see the rear tires of the car ahead when you stop.

Glossary: roundabout (a one-way circular intersection where entering traffic yields to circulating traffic); lane hopping (continual lane changing); following interval (the time gap to the vehicle ahead, measured by counting); blind spot (the area beside the vehicle not shown in the mirrors); downshifting (selecting a lower gear while moving); double clutching (matching engine speed for a non-synchronized downshift).

Dynamic facts: none; the maneuver procedures and the unattended-child rule are stable content of this printing.
